items.stem: Which cation gives a light blue precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide?
items.answer: Cu²⁺
items.markingKey: Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂, light blue, insoluble in excess.

items.stem: Explain why a flame test cannot distinguish between solutions of sodium chloride and sodium sulfate.
items.answer: The flame colour is due to the cation; both contain Na⁺ (yellow); an anion test is needed.

items.stem: Explain why aqueous sodium hydroxide alone cannot distinguish between Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ ions.
items.answer: Both give a white precipitate that dissolves in excess NaOH to form a colourless solution.

items.stem: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing calcium ions. Describe what is seen, including when excess is added, and write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate.
items.answer: White precipitate, insoluble in excess; Ca²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Ca(OH)₂(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark colour of precipitate; 1 mark behaviour in excess; 1 mark ionic equation; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: Three solutions X, Y and Z each contain one cation. Results — X: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — no precipitate or very slight white precipitate; Y: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; NH₃(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; Z: NaOH(aq) — red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess. Identify the cation in each solution.
items.answer: X Ca²⁺ (calcium); Y Zn²⁺ (zinc); Z Fe³⁺ (iron(III))

items.stem: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing zinc ions. Describe what is seen, including when excess is added, and write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate.
items.answer: White precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; Zn²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Zn(OH)₂(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark colour of precipitate; 1 mark behaviour in excess; 1 mark ionic equation; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: A solution of an unknown salt is divided into three portions for testing. (a) Write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate. (b) Predict what would be seen with aqueous ammonia.
items.answer: (a) Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s) (b) red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess

items.stem: Yusuf is given an unlabelled solution of a salt in a chemistry club and tests it with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia. (a) Describe how aqueous sodium hydroxide should be added, and why. (b) Explain why a flame test would not help identify this ion. (c) Describe how to carry out a flame test.
items.answer: (a) A few drops at a time, then in excess, observing after each addition — to see whether any precipitate dissolves in excess. (b) This ion has no characteristic flame colour in the syllabus; use precipitate tests instead. (c) Dip a clean nichrome wire (cleaned with conc. HCl) into the solid, hold in a blue Bunsen flame, observe colour.

items.stem: Which two cations give white precipitates with aqueous sodium hydroxide that dissolve in excess?
items.answer: Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺
items.markingKey: Both hydroxides are amphoteric; Ca(OH)₂ does not dissolve in excess.

items.stem: How can Al³⁺ and Zn²⁺ be distinguished?
options: Add excess aqueous ammonia: only the zinc hydroxide dissolves
Add sodium hydroxide: only Al³⁺ gives a precipitate
items.answer: Add excess aqueous ammonia: only the zinc hydroxide dissolves
items.markingKey: Zn(OH)₂ dissolves in excess NH₃(aq); Al(OH)₃ does not.

items.stem: Explain why the precipitate formed from a solution of Fe²⁺ ions slowly turns brown at its surface.
items.answer: Iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised by air to iron(III) hydroxide (red-brown).

items.stem: Explain why a nichrome or platinum wire is cleaned with concentrated hydrochloric acid before a flame test.
items.answer: To remove traces of other metal ions that would contaminate the flame colour.

items.stem: Three solutions X, Y and Z each contain one cation. Results — X: NaOH(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; Y: NaOH(aq) — green precipitate, soluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; Z: NaOH(aq) — light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — light blue precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a dark blue solution. Identify the cation in each solution.
items.answer: X Fe²⁺ (iron(II)); Y Cr³⁺ (chromium(III)); Z Cu²⁺ (copper(II))

items.stem: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing iron(II) ions. Describe what is seen, including when excess is added, and write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate.
items.answer: Green precipitate, insoluble in excess; Fe²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₂(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark colour of precipitate; 1 mark behaviour in excess; 1 mark ionic equation; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: Three solutions X, Y and Z each contain one cation. Results — X: NaOH(aq) — light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — light blue precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a dark blue solution; Y: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; NH₃(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; Z: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; NH₃(aq) — white precipitate, insoluble in excess. Identify the cation in each solution.
items.answer: X Cu²⁺ (copper(II)); Y Zn²⁺ (zinc); Z Al³⁺ (aluminium)

items.stem: Mohammed is given an unlabelled solution of a salt in a college laboratory and tests it with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aqueous ammonia. (a) State the expected flame test colour. (b) Describe how to carry out a flame test.
items.answer: (a) orange-red (b) Dip a clean nichrome wire (cleaned with conc. HCl) into the solid, hold in a blue Bunsen flame, observe colour.

items.stem: A solution of an unknown salt is divided into three portions for testing. (a) The solution gave a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, insoluble in excess. Identify the cation, explaining your reasoning. (b) State the expected flame test colour. (c) Describe how to carry out a flame test.
items.answer: (a) Ca²⁺ (calcium) (b) orange-red (c) Dip a clean nichrome wire (cleaned with conc. HCl) into the solid, hold in a blue Bunsen flame, observe colour.

items.stem: Which reagent is used to test for sulfate ions after acidifying with dilute nitric acid?
items.answer: aqueous barium nitrate

items.stem: Explain why dilute hydrochloric acid must not be used to acidify a solution before testing for chloride ions with silver nitrate.
items.answer: It adds chloride ions, which would always give a white precipitate (false positive).

items.stem: Explain why dilute sulfuric acid must not be used to acidify a solution before the sulfate test.
items.answer: It contains sulfate ions, so a white precipitate would form whether or not the sample contained sulfate.

items.stem: A solid salt S is dissolved in water. Test 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a green precipitate, soluble in excess. Test 2: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate: white precipitate. Identify salt S and explain how each result leads to your answer.
items.answer: chromium(III) sulfate: test 1 shows Cr³⁺; test 2 shows SO₄²⁻.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cation; 1 mark anion; 1 mark name of salt [3]

items.stem: A solid salt S is dissolved in water. Test 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess. Test 2: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: white precipitate. Identify salt S and explain how each result leads to your answer.
items.answer: copper(II) chloride: test 1 shows Cu²⁺; test 2 shows Cl⁻.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cation; 1 mark anion; 1 mark name of salt [3]

items.stem: A student must plan tests to identify the anions in two unlabelled salts. (a) Write the ionic equation for the positive iodide test. (b) Name the gas produced in the test for nitrate ions and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s) (b) Ammonia: turns damp red litmus paper blue.

items.stem: What colour precipitate does an iodide give with acidified aqueous silver nitrate?
items.answer: yellow
items.markingKey: Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow.

items.stem: Explain why the test for nitrate ions must be carried out only after checking that ammonium ions are absent.
items.answer: Ammonium ions also release ammonia when warmed with NaOH, giving a false positive.

items.stem: Explain why the precipitate in the silver nitrate test does not tell you which metal ion is present.
items.answer: The precipitate is a silver halide; the anion is identified, not the cation of the original salt.

items.stem: Acidified aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution and a yellow precipitate forms. Identify the ion and write the ionic equation with state symbols.
items.answer: iodide (I⁻); Ag⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) → AgI(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark ion; 1 mark equation; 1 mark state symbols [3]

items.stem: A student must plan tests to identify the anions in two unlabelled salts. (a) Write the ionic equation for the positive sulfate test. (b) Explain why the solution is acidified before testing with barium nitrate.
items.answer: (a) Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s) (b) To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate (barium carbonate).

items.stem: Chloe is given two solids, A and B. A contains CO₃²⁻ ions and B contains NO₃⁻ ions, but the labels have fallen off. (a) Describe a test for carbonate ions and its result. (b) Describe a test for nitrate ions and its result.
items.answer: (a) Add dilute acid and test the gas with limewater: effervescence; carbon dioxide turns limewater milky. (b) Add aqueous sodium hydroxide, then aluminium foil; warm carefully: ammonia gas produced, which turns damp red litmus paper blue.

items.stem: A student must plan tests to identify the anions in two unlabelled salts. (a) Describe a test for sulfite ions and its result. (b) Explain why the solution is acidified before testing with barium nitrate. (c) Name the gas produced in the test for nitrate ions and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Add dilute hydrochloric acid, warm gently and test the gas with acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII): sulfur dioxide produced, which turns acidified potassium manganate(VII) from purple to colourless. (b) To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate (barium carbonate). (c) Ammonia: turns damp red litmus paper blue.

items.stem: Which gas relights a glowing splint?
items.answer: oxygen

items.stem: Explain why litmus paper must be damp when testing for ammonia.
items.answer: Ammonia must dissolve in water to form an alkaline solution (OH⁻ ions) to change the indicator colour.

items.stem: Explain why limewater turns milky with carbon dioxide.
items.answer: CO₂ reacts with calcium hydroxide to form insoluble calcium carbonate, a white precipitate.

items.stem: A gas is produced from electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (at the anode). Name the gas and describe a test to confirm its identity, giving the result.
items.answer: chlorine; damp litmus paper is bleached.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gas; 1 mark test; 1 mark result [3]

items.stem: A gas is produced from calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid. Name the gas and describe a test to confirm its identity, giving the result.
items.answer: carbon dioxide; limewater turns milky.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gas; 1 mark test; 1 mark result [3]

items.stem: Chloe carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) sodium sulfite warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid; (2) calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid; (3) hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide. (a) Describe the test for the gas from reaction (2). (b) Write an equation for reaction (1).
items.answer: (a) limewater turns milky (b) Na₂SO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + SO₂

items.stem: Explain why hydrogen gives a "squeaky pop" with a lighted splint.
items.answer: Hydrogen reacts rapidly (explodes) with oxygen from the air to form water.

items.stem: Explain why the test for chlorine must be done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: Chlorine is toxic.

items.stem: Two gas jars contain ammonia and carbon dioxide. Describe one test that would identify each gas, giving the results you would expect.
items.answer: Ammonia: damp red litmus paper turns blue. Carbon dioxide: limewater turns milky.

items.stem: A gas is produced from sodium sulfite warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid. Name the gas and describe a test to confirm its identity, giving the result.
items.answer: sulfur dioxide; acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) turns from purple to colourless.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gas; 1 mark test; 1 mark result [3]

items.stem: Freya carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) magnesium and dilute sulfuric acid; (2) electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (at the anode); (3) calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid. (a) Suggest which gas should only be tested in a fume cupboard and why. (b) Write an equation for reaction (1).
items.answer: (a) Chlorine, sulfur dioxide or ammonia — they are toxic/irritants. (b) Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂

items.stem: Noah carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) magnesium and dilute sulfuric acid; (2) ammonium chloride warmed with sodium hydroxide; (3) calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid. (a) Describe the test for the gas from reaction (1). (b) Suggest which gas should only be tested in a fume cupboard and why. (c) Describe how a gas that is less dense than air and insoluble in water could be collected.
items.answer: (a) a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop (b) Chlorine, sulfur dioxide or ammonia — they are toxic/irritants. (c) Over water in an inverted measuring cylinder, or by upward delivery, or in a gas syringe.

items.stem: Daniel carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) calcium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid; (2) electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (at the anode); (3) hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide. (a) Name the gas produced in each reaction. (b) Describe how a gas that is less dense than air and insoluble in water could be collected. (c) Write an equation for reaction (1).
items.answer: (a) (1) carbon dioxide; (2) chlorine; (3) oxygen (b) Over water in an inverted measuring cylinder, or by upward delivery, or in a gas syringe. (c) CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂

items.stem: What colour is methyl orange in an acidic solution?
items.answer: red
items.markingKey: Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in alkali, orange at the end-point.

items.stem: Explain why the conical flask is rinsed with distilled water but the burette is rinsed with the acid.
items.answer: Water in the flask does not change the number of moles of alkali added by pipette; water in the burette would dilute the acid and change its concentration.

items.stem: Explain why titrations are repeated until concordant results are obtained.
items.answer: To make sure results are reliable/repeatable; concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³) are averaged.

items.stem: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of 0.0500 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide required 15.20 cm³ of hydrochloric acid for neutralisation. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.0822 mol/dm³

items.stem: In a titration, 10.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide required 18.75 cm³ of hydrochloric acid for neutralisation. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.0800 mol/dm³

items.stem: Kwame determines the concentration of sodium hydroxide by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.100 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, using methyl orange. Burette readings (initial → final, cm³): rough: 3.10 → 27.00; run 1: 1.20 → 24.35; run 2: 2.35 → 25.05; run 3: 2.35 → 25.45. (a) Describe how 25.0 cm³ of the alkali is measured into the flask. (b) Explain why universal indicator is not suitable. (c) Explain why the rough titre is not included in the mean.
items.answer: (a) Use a volumetric pipette (rinsed with the alkali) with a pipette filler; read at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. (b) It changes colour gradually; no sharp end-point. (c) It overshoots/ is only approximate.

items.stem: What colour is thymolphthalein in an alkaline solution?
items.answer: blue
items.markingKey: Thymolphthalein: colourless in acid, blue in alkali.

items.stem: Explain why the burette tap must be filled below the tap (no air bubble) before starting.
items.answer: An air bubble would leave the jet during the titration, making the measured volume larger than the volume delivered.

items.stem: Explain why phenolphthalein-type indicators such as thymolphthalein are colourless at the end-point when acid is added to alkali.
items.answer: The alkali has been just neutralised; the indicator changes from blue to colourless as the pH falls below its range.

items.stem: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide required 24.60 cm³ of sulfuric acid for neutralisation. H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.102 mol/dm³

items.stem: In a titration, 20.0 cm³ of 0.0800 mol/dm³ sodium hydroxide required 15.20 cm³ of hydrochloric acid for neutralisation. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.105 mol/dm³

items.stem: Hana determines the concentration of sodium hydroxide by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.150 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid, using methyl orange. Burette readings (initial → final, cm³): rough: 0.50 → 22.95; run 1: 0.50 → 22.15; run 2: 3.10 → 24.80; run 3: 0.50 → 22.20. (a) Describe how 25.0 cm³ of the alkali is measured into the flask. (b) Suggest why a white tile is used.
items.answer: (a) Use a volumetric pipette (rinsed with the alkali) with a pipette filler; read at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. (b) To see the colour change clearly.

items.stem: What colour is the flame test for potassium ions?
items.answer: lilac
items.markingKey: K⁺ lilac; Na⁺ yellow; Li⁺ red; Ca²⁺ orange-red; Ba²⁺ light green; Cu²⁺ blue-green.

items.stem: Describe a test to distinguish between solutions containing NH₄⁺ ions and Na⁺ ions. Give the result for each.
items.answer: Warm with aqueous NaOH: only NH₄⁺ releases ammonia, turning damp red litmus blue.

items.stem: Describe a test to distinguish between solutions containing Zn²⁺ ions and Ca²⁺ ions. Give the result for each.
items.answer: Add excess aqueous sodium hydroxide: zinc hydroxide dissolves, calcium hydroxide does not; or aqueous ammonia gives a white precipitate only with Zn²⁺.

items.stem: Three solutions X, Y and Z each contain one cation. Results — X: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; NH₃(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; Y: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — no precipitate or very slight white precipitate; Z: NaOH(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess. Identify the cation in each solution.
items.answer: X Zn²⁺ (zinc); Y Ca²⁺ (calcium); Z Fe²⁺ (iron(II))

items.stem: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing aluminium ions. Describe what is seen, including when excess is added, and write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate.
items.answer: White precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; Al³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Al(OH)₃(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark colour of precipitate; 1 mark behaviour in excess; 1 mark ionic equation; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: A water sample from a mine in Karachi is tested for metal ions. (a) The solution gave a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution. Identify the cation, explaining your reasoning. (b) Describe how to carry out a flame test.
items.answer: (a) Zn²⁺ (zinc) — confirm with aqueous ammonia (b) Dip a clean nichrome wire (cleaned with conc. HCl) into the solid, hold in a blue Bunsen flame, observe colour.

items.stem: Why is the solution acidified with nitric acid before adding silver nitrate?
options: To change the colour of the precipitate
To remove carbonate ions that would also give a precipitate
items.answer: To remove carbonate ions that would also give a precipitate
items.markingKey: Carbonate would precipitate silver carbonate, giving a false positive.

items.stem: Describe a test for carbonate ions in a solution, giving the reagent(s) and the positive result.
items.answer: Add dilute acid and test the gas with limewater: effervescence; carbon dioxide turns limewater milky.

items.stem: A solid salt S is dissolved in water. Test 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a green precipitate, soluble in excess. Test 2: add aqueous sodium hydroxide, then aluminium foil; warm carefully: ammonia gas produced, which turns damp red litmus paper blue. Identify salt S and explain how each result leads to your answer.
items.answer: chromium(III) nitrate: test 1 shows Cr³⁺; test 2 shows NO₃⁻.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cation; 1 mark anion; 1 mark name of salt [3]

items.stem: A solid salt S is dissolved in water. Test 1: aqueous sodium hydroxide gives a light blue precipitate, insoluble in excess. Test 2: add aqueous sodium hydroxide, then aluminium foil; warm carefully: ammonia gas produced, which turns damp red litmus paper blue. Identify salt S and explain how each result leads to your answer.
items.answer: copper(II) nitrate: test 1 shows Cu²⁺; test 2 shows NO₃⁻.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cation; 1 mark anion; 1 mark name of salt [3]

items.stem: A student must plan tests to identify the anions in two unlabelled salts. (a) Describe a test for bromide ions and its result. (b) Describe a test for chloride ions and its result. (c) Explain why the solution is acidified before testing with barium nitrate.
items.answer: (a) Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: cream precipitate. (b) Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: white precipitate. (c) To remove carbonate ions, which would also form a white precipitate (barium carbonate).

items.stem: A gas is tested with a lighted splint, which gives a squeaky pop. Which gas is it?
items.answer: hydrogen
items.markingKey: hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: Two gas jars contain sulfur dioxide and ammonia. Describe one test that would identify each gas, giving the results you would expect.
items.answer: Sulfur dioxide: acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) turns from purple to colourless. Ammonia: damp red litmus paper turns blue.

items.stem: A gas is produced from ammonium chloride warmed with sodium hydroxide. Name the gas and describe a test to confirm its identity, giving the result.
items.answer: ammonia; damp red litmus paper turns blue.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gas; 1 mark test; 1 mark result [3]

items.stem: A gas is produced from zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid. Name the gas and describe a test to confirm its identity, giving the result.
items.answer: hydrogen; a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gas; 1 mark test; 1 mark result [3]

items.stem: Ravi carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (at the anode); (2) magnesium and dilute sulfuric acid; (3) ammonium chloride warmed with sodium hydroxide. (a) Name the gas produced in each reaction. (b) Describe how a gas that is less dense than air and insoluble in water could be collected. (c) Write an equation for reaction (1).
items.answer: (a) (1) chlorine; (2) hydrogen; (3) ammonia (b) Over water in an inverted measuring cylinder, or by upward delivery, or in a gas syringe. (c) 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻

items.stem: During a titration, Jonas left an air bubble in the burette jet that disappeared during the titration. Predict the effect on the titre and explain.
items.answer: Titre larger: The reading change includes the bubble volume, so the recorded titre is larger than the acid actually added.

items.stem: During a titration, Lina rinsed the pipette with distilled water just before measuring the alkali. Predict the effect on the titre and explain.
items.answer: Titre smaller: The alkali is diluted, so fewer moles are added and less acid is needed.

items.stem: In a titration, 25.0 cm³ of 0.0800 mol/dm³ potassium hydroxide required 18.75 cm³ of hydrochloric acid for neutralisation. HCl + KOH → KCl + H₂O. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.107 mol/dm³

items.stem: Diego determines the concentration of sodium hydroxide by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.150 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid, using thymolphthalein. Burette readings (initial → final, cm³): rough: 0.50 → 26.45; run 1: 0.50 → 25.65; run 2: 0.80 → 26.00; run 3: 1.20 → 26.40. (a) State the colour change at the end-point. (b) Explain why universal indicator is not suitable. (c) Suggest why a white tile is used. (d) Explain why the rough titre is not included in the mean.
items.answer: (a) blue to colourless (b) It changes colour gradually; no sharp end-point. (c) To see the colour change clearly. (d) It overshoots/ is only approximate.

items.stem: Which test identifies the ammonium ion?
options: Warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide and test the gas with damp red litmus paper
items.answer: Warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide and test the gas with damp red litmus paper
items.markingKey: NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O; ammonia turns damp red litmus blue.

items.stem: Describe a test to distinguish between solutions containing Fe²⁺ ions and Fe³⁺ ions. Give the result for each.
items.answer: Add aqueous sodium hydroxide: Fe²⁺ gives a green precipitate, Fe³⁺ a red-brown precipitate.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why a nichrome or platinum wire is cleaned with concentrated hydrochloric acid before a flame test. (b) Explain why the precipitate formed from a solution of Fe²⁺ ions slowly turns brown at its surface.
items.answer: (a) To remove traces of other metal ions that would contaminate the flame colour. (b) Iron(II) hydroxide is oxidised by air to iron(III) hydroxide (red-brown).

items.stem: Three solutions X, Y and Z each contain one cation. Results — X: NaOH(aq) — red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess; Y: NaOH(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; NH₃(aq) — green precipitate, insoluble in excess; Z: NaOH(aq) — white precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a colourless solution; NH₃(aq) — white precipitate, insoluble in excess. Identify the cation in each solution.
items.answer: X Fe³⁺ (iron(III)); Y Fe²⁺ (iron(II)); Z Al³⁺ (aluminium)

items.stem: Aqueous sodium hydroxide is added to a solution containing iron(III) ions. Describe what is seen, including when excess is added, and write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of the precipitate.
items.answer: Red-brown precipitate, insoluble in excess; Fe³⁺(aq) + 3OH⁻(aq) → Fe(OH)₃(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark colour of precipitate; 1 mark behaviour in excess; 1 mark ionic equation; 1 mark state symbols [4]

items.stem: A water sample from a mine in Doha is tested for metal ions. (a) Write the ionic equation for the formation of the precipitate. (b) Predict what would be seen with aqueous ammonia.
items.answer: (a) Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)₂(s) (b) light blue precipitate, soluble in excess, giving a dark blue solution

items.stem: Which test shows the presence of nitrate ions?
options: Warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil; ammonia is produced
items.answer: Warm with aqueous sodium hydroxide and aluminium foil; ammonia is produced
items.markingKey: NO₃⁻ is reduced to NH₃, which turns damp red litmus blue.

items.stem: Describe a test for sulfate ions in a solution, giving the reagent(s) and the positive result.
items.answer: Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate: white precipitate.

items.stem: A solid salt S is dissolved in water. Test 1: flame test colour lilac. Test 2: acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous barium nitrate: white precipitate. Identify salt S and explain how each result leads to your answer.
items.answer: potassium sulfate: test 1 shows K⁺; test 2 shows SO₄²⁻.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cation; 1 mark anion; 1 mark name of salt [3]

items.stem: Acidified aqueous silver nitrate is added to a solution and a white precipitate forms. Identify the ion and write the ionic equation with state symbols.
items.answer: chloride (Cl⁻); Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s)
items.markingKey: 1 mark ion; 1 mark equation; 1 mark state symbols [3]

items.stem: A laboratory in Cairo needs to confirm the anions present in two fertiliser samples. (a) Describe a test for iodide ions and its result. (b) Write the ionic equation for the positive bromide test. (c) Explain why nitric acid, rather than hydrochloric acid, is used to acidify a solution before adding silver nitrate.
items.answer: (a) Acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add aqueous silver nitrate: yellow precipitate. (b) Ag⁺(aq) + Br⁻(aq) → AgBr(s) (c) HCl adds chloride ions that would form a white precipitate.

items.stem: A gas is tested with a glowing splint, which relights. Which gas is it?
items.answer: oxygen

items.stem: Two gas jars contain chlorine and carbon dioxide. Describe one test that would identify each gas, giving the results you would expect.
items.answer: Chlorine: damp litmus paper is bleached. Carbon dioxide: limewater turns milky.

items.stem: A gas is produced from hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide. Name the gas and describe a test to confirm its identity, giving the result.
items.answer: oxygen; a glowing splint relights.
items.markingKey: 1 mark gas; 1 mark test; 1 mark result [3]

items.stem: Kwame carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) ammonium chloride warmed with sodium hydroxide; (2) sodium sulfite warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid; (3) zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid. (a) Describe the test for the gas from reaction (2). (b) Describe how a gas that is less dense than air and insoluble in water could be collected.
items.answer: (a) acidified aqueous potassium manganate(VII) turns from purple to colourless (b) Over water in an inverted measuring cylinder, or by upward delivery, or in a gas syringe.

items.stem: Mohammed carries out three reactions and collects the gases: (1) sodium sulfite warmed with dilute hydrochloric acid; (2) hydrogen peroxide with manganese(IV) oxide; (3) ammonium chloride warmed with sodium hydroxide. (a) Name the gas produced in each reaction. (b) Describe the test for the gas from reaction (2). (c) Describe how a gas that is less dense than air and insoluble in water could be collected.
items.answer: (a) (1) sulfur dioxide; (2) oxygen; (3) ammonia (b) a glowing splint relights (c) Over water in an inverted measuring cylinder, or by upward delivery, or in a gas syringe.

items.stem: During a titration, Hana added extra distilled water to the conical flask. Predict the effect on the titre and explain.
items.answer: Titre unchanged: The number of moles of alkali is unchanged, so the same volume of acid is needed.

items.stem: During a titration, Ines overshot the end-point by adding acid too quickly. Predict the effect on the titre and explain.
items.answer: Titre larger: More acid than needed was added before the colour change was noticed.

items.stem: In a titration, 20.0 cm³ of 0.200 mol/dm³ sodium carbonate required 24.60 cm³ of sulfuric acid for neutralisation. H₂SO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂. Calculate the concentration of the acid.
items.answer: 0.163 mol/dm³

items.stem: Hana determines the concentration of potassium hydroxide by titrating 25.0 cm³ portions with 0.120 mol/dm³ nitric acid, using thymolphthalein. Burette readings (initial → final, cm³): rough: 1.20 → 21.70; run 1: 1.05 → 20.85; run 2: 1.20 → 21.00; run 3: 0.00 → 19.85. (a) Describe how 25.0 cm³ of the alkali is measured into the flask. (b) State the colour change at the end-point. (c) Explain why universal indicator is not suitable.
items.answer: (a) Use a volumetric pipette (rinsed with the alkali) with a pipette filler; read at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level. (b) blue to colourless (c) It changes colour gradually; no sharp end-point.
